primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Factor V Leiden thrombophilia due to an F5 variant causing resistance to activated protein C
mechanism: Activated factor V normally serves as a procoagulant cofactor and is inactivated by proteolytic cleavage by activated protein C. The factor V Leiden F5 variant alters a critical APC cleavage site, slowing factor V inactivation, prolonging thrombin generation, and creating a hereditary hypercoagulable state.
vignette: A 27-year-old woman has a second unprovoked deep venous thrombosis. Her father had a pulmonary embolism at age 38. Platelet count, PT, and aPTT are normal. A functional assay shows reduced anticoagulant response after addition of activated protein C.
distractors: Antithrombin deficiency
Protein C deficiency
Antiphospholipid syndrome
Prothrombin G20210A thrombophilia
distractor_notes: Antithrombin deficiency causes hereditary venous thrombosis but does not specifically produce an activated-protein-C resistance assay.
Protein C deficiency reduces generation of an anticoagulant protease; it is distinct from resistance of factor V to APC-mediated cleavage.
Antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired thrombophilia commonly associated with lupus anticoagulant/anticardiolipin antibodies and may prolong phospholipid-dependent clotting assays.
Prothrombin G20210A increases prothrombin levels but does not cause APC resistance.
key_expl: Recurrent venous thrombosis at a young age, a familial pattern, and reduced response to activated protein C strongly identify factor V Leiden thrombophilia. The F5 variant makes activated factor V resistant to normal APC-mediated inactivation.
objective: Recognize factor V Leiden from hereditary venous thrombosis and activated-protein-C resistance, and connect the phenotype to impaired APC cleavage of factor V.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Constrictive pericarditis from a rigid noncompliant pericardium limiting diastolic expansion
mechanism: A thickened, fibrotic, noncompliant pericardium abruptly limits ventricular expansion during diastole. Venous return increases during inspiration but the right ventricle cannot accommodate the additional volume, so systemic venous pressure fails to fall and may rise, producing Kussmaul sign; abrupt cessation of rapid early filling can generate a pericardial knock.
vignette: A 58-year-old man with prior mediastinal radiation has progressive edema, ascites, and exertional fatigue. Jugular venous pressure rises during inspiration. Cardiac auscultation reveals an early diastolic pericardial knock. CT shows a thickened calcified pericardium.
lead: Which physiologic abnormality most directly explains the inspiratory rise in jugular venous pressure?
correct: Failure of the right ventricle to expand adequately because the rigid pericardium limits diastolic filling
distractors: Excessive inspiratory increase in left ventricular afterload from systemic vasoconstriction
Dynamic obstruction of right ventricular outflow during inspiration
Loss of atrioventricular nodal delay with premature ventricular filling
Marked inspiratory reduction in venous return to the right atrium
distractor_notes: Systemic afterload changes do not explain the classic Kussmaul sign of constrictive physiology.
Right ventricular outflow obstruction is not the mechanism produced by a fibrotic, noncompliant pericardium.
AV nodal timing is unrelated to the impaired ventricular compliance caused by constriction.
Inspiration normally increases systemic venous return; the abnormality is inability of the constrained right ventricle to accept that increased return.
key_expl: Kussmaul sign in constrictive pericarditis reflects the failure of right-sided filling to increase normally during inspiration because a rigid pericardium limits ventricular expansion.
objective: Explain Kussmaul sign in constrictive pericarditis as impaired accommodation of inspiratory venous return due to a noncompliant pericardium.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: VIPoma causing watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and hypochlorhydria through excessive vasoactive intestinal peptide secretion
mechanism: VIP binds VPAC G-protein-coupled receptors and increases intracellular cAMP in intestinal epithelial and smooth-muscle target tissues. Excess VIP drives intestinal water, electrolyte, and bicarbonate secretion while inhibiting gastric acid secretion, producing fasting-persistent secretory diarrhea, hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis, and hypochlorhydria.
vignette: A 46-year-old woman has several months of profuse watery diarrhea that continues despite a 48-hour fast. She has muscle weakness and dehydration. Laboratory studies show hypokalemia and a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Gastric acid secretion is markedly reduced, and abdominal imaging shows a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.
distractors: Insulinoma
Gastrinoma
Somatostatinoma
Glucagonoma
distractor_notes: Insulinoma causes recurrent fasting hypoglycemia rather than high-volume secretory diarrhea.
Gastrinoma causes gastric acid hypersecretion and peptic ulcer disease, opposite the reduced acid secretion described.

Somatostatinoma is associated with diabetes, steatorrhea, gallstones, and hypochlorhydria but does not classically cause the severe fasting-persistent watery diarrhea and profound hypokalemia of VIP excess.
Glucagonoma causes diabetes, weight loss, venous thrombosis, and necrolytic migratory erythema rather than WDHA physiology.
key_expl: Fasting-persistent secretory diarrhea, profound hypokalemia, bicarbonate loss with metabolic acidosis, hypochlorhydria, and a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor are classic for VIPoma (WDHA syndrome).
objective: Recognize VIPoma from fasting-persistent secretory diarrhea, hypokalemia, bicarbonate loss, and hypochlorhydria and connect the syndrome to excessive VIP-cAMP signaling.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Primary hyperaldosteronism with autonomous aldosterone excess
mechanism: Autonomous aldosterone excess increases ENaC-mediated sodium entry in collecting-duct principal cells and enhances basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase activity, creating a lumen-negative potential that favors potassium secretion through ROMK. Aldosterone also promotes hydrogen secretion by alpha-intercalated cells, producing hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis while volume expansion suppresses renin.
vignette: A 43-year-old woman has resistant hypertension, muscle weakness, serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L, and metabolic alkalosis. Plasma renin activity is suppressed and aldosterone concentration is elevated.
lead: Which renal change most directly contributes to this patient's hypokalemia?
correct: Increased ENaC-mediated sodium reabsorption in principal cells, increasing the electrical drive for potassium secretion
distractors: Reduced proximal tubular sodium reabsorption causing bicarbonaturia
Reduced NKCC2 activity in the thick ascending limb
Reduced distal sodium delivery to collecting-duct principal cells
Inhibition of basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase in collecting-duct principal cells
distractor_notes: Proximal bicarbonate loss causes metabolic acidosis rather than the aldosterone-associated alkalosis described.
Reduced NKCC2 activity produces Bartter physiology with secondary hyperaldosteronism, not suppressed renin from autonomous aldosterone excess.
Aldosterone-driven sodium retention does not reduce the relevant epithelial sodium entry; ENaC activity is increased.
Aldosterone increases, rather than inhibits, principal-cell sodium-potassium exchange processes that favor potassium secretion.
key_expl: In primary hyperaldosteronism, aldosterone upregulates ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase. Enhanced electrogenic sodium reabsorption makes the lumen more negative and drives potassium secretion, producing hypokalemia.
objective: Connect autonomous aldosterone excess to ENaC-mediated collecting-duct sodium reabsorption, potassium wasting, metabolic alkalosis, and suppressed renin.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Cystinuria from defective proximal tubular reabsorption of cystine and dibasic amino acids
mechanism: SLC3A1 and SLC7A9 encode the two subunits of an apical heteromeric transporter in renal proximal tubular epithelial cells and the small intestine. Loss of transporter function impairs reabsorption of cystine and dibasic amino acids; poorly soluble cystine precipitates in urine and forms recurrent stones.
vignette: A 16-year-old boy has recurrent nephrolithiasis. Urine microscopy shows flat colorless hexagonal crystals. A cyanide-nitroprusside test is positive. Serum amino acid concentrations are otherwise unremarkable.
lead: Which transport defect most directly causes this disorder?
correct: Reduced proximal tubular reabsorption of cystine and dibasic amino acids
distractors: Reduced collecting-duct reabsorption of water through aquaporin-2
Reduced proximal tubular reabsorption of glucose through SGLT2
Reduced thick-ascending-limb reabsorption of sodium, potassium, and chloride
Reduced distal convoluted tubular reabsorption of calcium through TRPV5
distractor_notes: Aquaporin-2 dysfunction causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus rather than cystine stones.
SGLT2 dysfunction causes renal glucosuria, not hexagonal cystine crystalluria.
NKCC2 defects cause Bartter syndrome with salt wasting and hypercalciuria, not selective dibasic aminoaciduria.
Distal calcium transport abnormalities alter calcium handling but do not cause the characteristic cystine transporter phenotype.
key_expl: Cystinuria results from pathogenic variants in SLC3A1 and/or SLC7A9, which form the apical transporter responsible for proximal tubular reabsorption of cystine and dibasic amino acids. Cystine's low solubility leads to hexagonal crystals and recurrent stones.
objective: Identify cystinuria as a proximal tubular cystine/dibasic-amino-acid transport defect caused by SLC3A1/SLC7A9 dysfunction.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Huntington disease with paternal anticipation from germline instability of the HTT CAG repeat
mechanism: Huntington disease is caused by expansion of a CAG repeat in HTT. Repeat length can increase across generations, and large expansions occur disproportionately during paternal transmission because the repeat is unstable during spermatogenesis; increasing repeat length is generally associated with earlier disease onset.
vignette: A 38-year-old man develops progressive chorea, irritability, and executive dysfunction. His father developed similar symptoms at age 55. Genetic testing shows an expanded HTT CAG repeat that is substantially longer in the son than in the father.
lead: Which process most directly explains the earlier onset in the son?
correct: Expansion of the CAG repeat during paternal germline transmission
distractors: Mitochondrial heteroplasmy with replicative segregation
Genomic imprinting that silences the maternal HTT allele
Somatic recombination deleting the normal HTT allele
X-chromosome inactivation skewing in the son
distractor_notes: Huntington disease is an autosomal-dominant trinucleotide-repeat disorder, not a mitochondrial heteroplasmy syndrome.
The anticipation effect is due to repeat instability rather than parent-specific silencing of an HTT allele.
Loss of the normal allele is not required to explain intergenerational anticipation.
HTT is autosomal, so X-chromosome inactivation is not relevant.
key_expl: Huntington anticipation reflects CAG-repeat instability. Expansion is especially common during paternal transmission, and larger expanded alleles are associated with earlier clinical onset.
objective: Explain paternal anticipation in Huntington disease as expansion of an unstable HTT CAG repeat during spermatogenesis.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
discipline: Genetics / Histology & Cell Biology / Biochemistry / Physiology
diagnosis: Duchenne muscular dystrophy caused by an out-of-frame DMD pathogenic variant with near-absence of functional dystrophin
mechanism: Out-of-frame deletions or other truncating DMD variants disrupt the translational reading frame, producing severely truncated unstable dystrophin that is degraded. Loss of dystrophin destabilizes the sarcolemma during contraction, causing repeated myofiber injury, high CK, progressive weakness, and replacement by fat/connective tissue.
vignette: A 4-year-old boy has difficulty running and climbing stairs. He uses his hands to push on his thighs when rising from the floor and has calf pseudohypertrophy. Creatine kinase is markedly elevated. Genetic testing shows a deletion of DMD exons that shifts the translational reading frame.
lead: Which molecular consequence best explains the severe phenotype?
correct: Production of a severely truncated unstable dystrophin protein that is rapidly degraded
distractors: Production of a shortened but partially functional in-frame dystrophin protein
Excess transcription of a structurally normal dystrophin gene
Failure of collagen type I secretion from skeletal-muscle fibroblasts
Constitutive activation of the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex
distractor_notes: In-frame deletions more often preserve partial dystrophin function and correlate with the milder Becker phenotype.
Duchenne disease reflects loss of functional dystrophin rather than excessive normal transcription.
Type I collagen secretion defects cause connective-tissue/bone disorders rather than an X-linked dystrophinopathy.
The dystrophin-associated complex becomes mechanically destabilized when dystrophin is absent; constitutive activation is not the primary defect.
key_expl: The reading-frame rule predicts that out-of-frame DMD variants usually produce severe Duchenne disease because they generate a truncated dystrophin that is degraded, leaving little or no functional protein.
objective: Use the dystrophin reading-frame rule to distinguish severe Duchenne disease from milder Becker disease and connect absent dystrophin to sarcolemmal instability.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Meckel diverticulum from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct
mechanism: The vitelline duct normally connects the embryonic midgut to the yolk sac and involutes during early development. Incomplete obliteration can leave a true ileal diverticulum; ectopic gastric mucosa may secrete acid, ulcerating adjacent ileal mucosa and causing painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding.
vignette: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent painless maroon-colored stools. Hemoglobin is decreased. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows focal tracer uptake in the right lower abdomen synchronous with gastric uptake.
lead: Persistence of which embryologic structure most directly caused this lesion?
distractors: Urachus
Allantois-derived median umbilical ligament
Dorsal mesogastrium
Cloacal membrane
distractor_notes: Persistent urachal tissue connects the bladder region to the umbilicus and causes urachal cysts or urinary drainage, not an ileal true diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa.
The median umbilical ligament is the adult urachal remnant and is unrelated to Meckel diverticulum.
The dorsal mesogastrium contributes structures associated with stomach rotation and the greater omentum rather than a distal ileal vitelline remnant.
The cloacal membrane is involved in terminal hindgut/urogenital development, not the embryonic connection between midgut and yolk sac.
key_expl: Meckel diverticulum is a persistent vitelline/omphalomesenteric duct remnant. Ectopic gastric mucosa can cause adjacent ileal ulceration and painless bleeding and is detected by a technetium pertechnetate scan.
objective: Identify Meckel diverticulum as a vitelline-duct remnant and connect ectopic gastric mucosa to painless pediatric gastrointestinal bleeding.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: VanA-mediated vancomycin resistance from replacement of D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac in peptidoglycan precursors
mechanism: Vancomycin binds the terminal D-alanyl-D-alanine motif of peptidoglycan precursors and sterically impairs cell-wall polymerization/cross-linking. VanA resistance remodels the precursor terminus to D-Ala-D-Lac, markedly reducing vancomycin binding affinity and allowing peptidoglycan synthesis to continue.
vignette: A hospitalized patient develops Enterococcus faecium bacteremia. The isolate is highly resistant to vancomycin and carries the vanA resistance cluster.
lead: Which molecular change most directly explains this resistance?
correct: Replacement of the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala sequence with D-Ala-D-Lac
distractors: Methylation of 23S ribosomal RNA
Hydrolysis of the beta-lactam ring by a plasmid-encoded enzyme
Mutation of DNA gyrase that reduces fluoroquinolone binding
Loss of folate synthesis due to dihydropteroate synthase inhibition
distractor_notes: 23S rRNA methylation mediates resistance to several macrolide/lincosamide/streptogramin drugs rather than classic VanA glycopeptide resistance.
Beta-lactamases confer resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics, not vancomycin.
DNA gyrase mutations are a mechanism of fluoroquinolone resistance.
Folate-pathway inhibition describes sulfonamide pharmacology and does not explain glycopeptide resistance.
key_expl: Vancomycin normally binds D-Ala-D-Ala on peptidoglycan precursors. VanA changes that terminus to D-Ala-D-Lac, sharply reducing drug affinity and producing high-level vancomycin resistance.
objective: Connect vancomycin's D-Ala-D-Ala target to VanA-mediated replacement with D-Ala-D-Lac and high-level enterococcal resistance.

diagnosis: Intention-to-treat analysis preserves the prognostic balance created by randomization by analyzing participants in their originally assigned groups
mechanism: Randomization balances measured and unmeasured prognostic factors on average. Intention-to-treat analysis retains participants in the groups to which they were randomized regardless of nonadherence, crossover, or protocol deviations, thereby preserving the main protection against selection bias conferred by random assignment.
vignette: In a randomized trial, 600 patients are assigned to a new antihypertensive drug or standard therapy. During follow-up, 12% of participants in each group stop their assigned therapy, and some cross over to the other treatment. Investigators want the primary efficacy analysis to preserve the benefits of the original randomization.
lead: Which analysis strategy is most appropriate?
correct: Analyze all participants according to their originally assigned treatment groups
distractors: Analyze only participants who completed the assigned therapy exactly as specified
Reassign crossover participants to the treatment they actually received
Exclude all participants who discontinued therapy before the final visit
Analyze only participants who achieved at least 80% medication adherence
distractor_notes: A per-protocol analysis can destroy prognostic balance because adherence itself may be related to outcome risk.
As-treated analysis breaks the original randomized comparison by regrouping participants according to post-randomization behavior.
Excluding discontinuations introduces selection/attrition bias and does not preserve the original groups.
Restricting analysis by adherence similarly conditions on a post-randomization characteristic and can bias treatment comparisons.
key_expl: Intention-to-treat analysis compares participants according to original random assignment, regardless of adherence or crossover. This preserves the prognostic balance created by randomization and limits selection bias introduced by post-randomization behavior.
objective: Identify intention-to-treat analysis as the preferred primary strategy for preserving randomization in trials with nonadherence or treatment crossover.
